#3341. ‘Superman’ Star’s New Heist Thriller Is Officially 2026's Latest Box Office Bomb

Nicholas Hoult has enjoyed a pretty remarkable run over the past few years, appearing in everything from The Menu and Nosferatu to James Gunn's Superman, where he stepped into the role of Lex Luthor. With a growing collection of major franchises and acclaimed performances under his belt, the British star has become one of Hollywood's most recognizable leading men. Unfortunately, that hasn't translated to box office success for his newest movie.

How to Rob a Bank has officially opened to just $5.175 million domestically across 2,810 theaters, making it one of Hoult's weakest wide-release debuts. The Amazon MGM Studios thriller also earned approximately $5.1 million internationally, bringing its worldwide total to $10.275 million following its first weekend in US theaters. The movie reportedly cost around $40 million to produce, meaning its opening represents a difficult start for a film that will need considerably more revenue to cover production and marketing expenses.

In How to Rob a Bank, Hoult is The Wolf, an anonymous YouTuber whose merry band of bank robbers — played by Pete Davidson, Anna Sawai, and Rhenzy Feliz — go viral broadcasting their heists on their channel. As they continue to garner more views, an FBI agent (John C. Reilly) enlists the help of a hacker under house arrest (Zoë Kravitz) to help track them down. Director David Leitch spoke to Collider's Steve Weintraub earlier this month about the inspiration behind the film, and how there's more to it than a simple cat-and-mouse thriller.

"It was very, very contemporary. I think these characters, although you don't really find out their motivations until the second act, which I've held off that reveal by choice, they're very relatable. People are dealing with health care debt, people are dealing with homes they can't afford, people are dealing with medical issues, and the system is not necessarily working for them."

Leitch added that he knew he still had to make the movie entertaining as well as informative, however, adding: "That's what art is supposed to do, and that's what this film is supposed to do, outside of it being a big, fun commercial heist movie. I think I set that up in the first act, but then I'm taking you on a journey."

How to Rob a Bank opened in US theaters on November 13, 2026, and is currently playing nationwide. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

#3335. The 10 Best Alternative Rock Albums of the 21st Century, Ranked

Looking over alternative rock music, most of the greatest of the greats can be found in the final couple of decades of the 20th century. Like, the 1980s and 1990s was the time when alternative rock was at its most classic and dominant, like how classic rock, you know, dominated (and felt “most” classic) in the second half of the 1960s and then throughout the 1970s.

That doesn’t mean you should only look to the 1980s and 1990s, though, if you want to hear great alternative rock. There have been more than enough artists tackling that genre so far throughout the 2000s and a little beyond as well. Case in point, these ones, which can count themselves among the very best alternative rock albums of the 21st century so far (more of them in the 2000s and the first half of the 2010s, sure, but rock – alternative or otherwise – just hasn’t thrived in quite the same way since about the mid-2010s onward).

It’s obvious to point at Interpol and say, “Hey, that band sounds quite a lot like Joy Division,” but maybe that’s okay. After all, there are only a couple of Joy Division albums, so there’s more territory with the whole post-punk sound to mine, but also, Interpol do some interesting things with that sound and aren’t just like a Joy Division cover band. Also, of course there’s going to be similarities, since Interpol are sometimes lumped in with the post-punk revival genre.

That’s what you'd expect it to be: post-punk returning with a bit of a sheen a couple of decades on from its heyday. Turn on the Bright Lights is the sort of definitive album you can listen to not just if you want to work out whether you'll like Interpol, but whether you'll like this whole sub-genre of alternative rock. It’s an album with a ton of hype behind it, but it thankfully lives up to all that.

Listing off highlights in terms of individual tracks feels hardest for Radiohead’s In Rainbows, owing to how well the album flows, and how consistent it is. Once you mention “15 Step,” “Weird Fishes/Arpeggi,” “Jigsaw Falling Into Place,” and “Videotape,” you feel obligated to mention all the other tracks, and that won’t be done. They're all great. They're all worthy of mentioning. That’s the main thing.

In Rainbows is a little more rock-adjacent, definitely came out in the 21st century, and it’s almost as good as Kid A, so it’s going here.

If Kid A counts as a 21st century album, then maybe it’s a little better than In Rainbows, but not by much. But the year 2000 is kind of the end of the 20th century rather than the start of the next one. Oh, and Kid A doesn’t have a lot by way of alternative rock. In Rainbows is a little more rock-adjacent, definitely came out in the 21st century, and it’s almost as good as Kid A, so it’s going here. It feels right.

Tame Impala is easily one of the best rock acts of the century so far, and it’s easier to call Tame Impala an act or a project than a band, since Tame Impala is – as the meme says – just one guy (Kevin Parker). The same can be said for The Cure (Robert Smith), though, so it’s not unheard of. Anyway, Tame Impala is great and/or Kevin Parker is great. Either way, same greatness.

Lonerism is the easiest album to label as “rock,” and probably the strongest overall, too, even if the slightly poppier Currents (2015) does have some undeniable highlights track-wise. Like, “Let It Happen” and “The Less I Know the Better” might be better than the best song on Lonerism, but Lonerism has extra appeal as a coherent album, with all its tracks bleeding into each other so well, making for a seamless listen for the 50-ish minutes it goes on for.

As the title might suggest, Songs for the Deaf is kind of a concept album, but not really the sort that goes far enough to have an in-depth narrative or a particularly notable number of themes it really hones in on. It’s more of an experience kind of thing, designed to replicate the feeling of cycling through a bunch of strange and/or unfamiliar radio stations during a long drive, and hey, it does do that premise/concept pretty well.

You’ve got a few interludes and snippets of audio contributing to this concept, but mostly, Songs for the Deaf stands out for being very generous with a ton of great alternative rock songs. Queens of the Stone Age peaked here, and that’s not so bad when the peak is this high (and, for what it’s worth, there are definitely other albums by the band worth checking out if you got something out of Songs for the Deaf).

You might not like this particular realization dawning on you, but if American Idiot were a person, it would've been able to drink legally for a year, and it’s been able to vote for about four years. It is old. Maybe that makes you feel old, too. But hey, it’s held up well. Maybe you’ve held up well, too. Best to stay positive (maybe not during September, though, if you want to be woken up when it ends).

American Idiot isn't really a positive album, though, for what it’s worth, since it’s an angry album, and one focused on reflecting feelings that were felt during a confusing and politically charged time in history. Time passes, though, and maybe even that simpler kind of anger and passion feels a little nostalgic. Anyway, this album is very much a time capsule for alternative rock in the 2000s, and maybe even the 2000s overall, so it’s well and truly got its place in history, all the while still sounding pretty great when listened to today.

Fever to Tell might be one of the best punk rock albums not released during that genre’s heyday, though it’s got a bit more to it than just punk, and so it fitting within the pantheon of great alternative rock albums also feels fitting. This Yeah Yeah Yeahs album definitely has that punk energy throughout, but its indie/alternative rock elements are implemented flawlessly, and it does indeed feel like rock a good deal of the time.

Counting the hidden track, there are 12 songs here, and the album isn't long, so the average track length is only about three minutes, meaning nothing really risks overstaying its welcome (a couple of songs even clock in at under two minutes in duration). Though it sounds of its time, Fever to Tell has aged surprisingly well and still sounds awesome, all the while also being able to count itself as easily the best album by Yeah Yeah Yeahs to date.

Quite a bit of what could be said about American Idiot can also be said about The Black Parade, with the two being rock operas/concept albums that blended alternative rock, pop, and a bit of punk. With The Black Parade, you can also lump it in with the emo genre, but it’s a cut above a ton of the other stuff associated with that particular genre/movement, all the while being the best and most ambitious of all the My Chemical Romance albums to date.

And then like American Idiot once again, nostalgia could have some impact on The Black Parade feeling as great as it does, but not wholly. The Black Parade is a genuinely great concept album dealing with all sorts of heavy things, and it goes more in-depth on those topics than you might expect, based on the genres it’s associated with. It’s something that was operating on a whole other level compared to all the comparable albums from around this time, and it’s aged exceedingly well all these years later.

The National had a good run throughout much of the first two decades of this current century. Like, there’s Alligator (2005) and Boxer (2007) often being fan favorites, and then the likes of Trouble Will Find Me (2013) and Sleep Well Beast (2017) are also excellent, being close to the standards of those other two albums. Yet you can see The National and their very best right between these two pairs of albums.

It’s High Violet (2010) that makes that halfway point, being a pretty much perfect album that encompasses everything great about The National within a single album. It is a somewhat dreary and downbeat listening experience, but there’s thankfully a lot of passion here alongside all the sadness, so it’s not miserable or too much. For something oftentimes sad, it’s also got a surprisingly high number of earworms and moments of catharsis.

With Arcade Fire, it’s a bit of a Radiohead kind of situation where the album here might not be the band’s very best, but it’s also not far off, and it’s here because it fits within the confines of “alternative rock” to the greatest extent. It’s The Suburbs, which is the band’s third album overall, and one where they really seem to tackle Americana, doing a bit of a Bruce Springsteen thing in parts alongside referencing and paying homage to some other great classic rock acts.

It’s eclectic, though, as can be expected from an Arcade Fire album, with the best song here sounding more like Blondie’s “Heart of Glass” than any classic rock song (the song in question is “Sprawl II (Mountains Beyond Mountains)”). Everything here is pretty great, though, and it could well be the most approachable album of the band’s, too.

If you're into indie/alternative rock, you'll pretty much guaranteed to like Wilco’s Yankee Hotel Foxtrot, but if you also like more old-fashioned sorts of rock, you'll likely also find things to like here. It’s just a great album, right up there with the century’s best so far, and that’s probably the easiest thing to say. It’s a more mellow sort of rock, sure, but rock nonetheless, maybe scratching a similar melancholic itch to some of the best The National albums.

Some sadness is inevitable when the album begins with a song named “I Am Trying to Break Your Heart,” so that one sets the stage quite ideally. Then there are other songs here that lyrically go beyond more personal topics like love, loss, and loneliness, with the variety being appreciated, of course. Some of the songs here are quite long, and Yankee Hotel Foxtrot also clocks in at over 50 minutes all up, but you never really come close to feeling the length here in a detrimental way.

#3334. Security Bite: Apple details Secure Exclaves, a glimpse at its ambient computing future

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

#3331. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, enabling ‘dot’ agents to make purchases

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a new bar for secure payments by agents.”

ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an issue online.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The company emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases.

Taking care of your espresso machine is easily overlooked, but these cute barista microfiber cloths bring a little sweetness back into cleaning. The embroidered coffee designs are whimsical and cute, and if I had these cloths, I would always remember to clean my machine.

At less than $1 a straw, this 14-pack of multicolored straws yearns for a place in my kitchen. The straws are shatter-resistant and even come with two pipe cleaners for easy maintenance.

I personally own De'Longhi's coffee glasses, and I adore them. The double-walled glass keeps coffee warmer for longer while being cool to the touch. These 3oz glasses are perfect for pulling shots like a pro.

The KitchenTour coffee scale is the cheapest coffee scale I've ever reviewed. It's big, it's reliable, and it's oh-so affordable. At under $20, this will have the coffee lover in your life nerding out over their espresso ratios without breaking the bank.

Ever get so locked in at work you forget about your coffee? Yeah, me too. This mug warmer keeps your drinks hot — between 130°F, 150°F, and 176°F — for up to 12 hours.

I hope my loved ones are reading this, because this is what I want. This coffee unit organizer holds your syrups, espresso equipment like tamper and WDT tool, and cleaning cloths without causing clutter.

If you want barista-beating latte art, you need a milk jug like this one with an angled spout. This Easyworkz model is $24 and can teach you how to get those florettes and tulips to a T.

If the KitchenTour Coffee Scale is a little big for your coffee lover's machine, don't fret. KitchenTour also makes a Mini, which weighs, times, and tares all the same. It's a little pricier, but smaller is worth those extra six bucks.

I rarely buy coffee syrups for myself, so I'd love a sampler assortment like this. You get all the standard flavors: vanilla, salted caramel, mocha, almond, pumpkin spice, and some unique ones like amaratti and peppermint.

This syrup sampler is even more festive, with flavors like tiramisu, cinnamon, toasted marshmallow, and gingerbread. I would run to the espresso machine after unwrapping this on Christmas morning.

Got an espresso nerd on your hands? Then, I'm sure they'll be plenty delighted by this Medieval-torture-device-looking thing: a WDT tool. This distributes coffee evenly in the portafilter basket (the silver thing where you put coffee before you put it in the espresso machine). Essential for any Nespresso machine owner, the Lume dispenser holds up to 30 Vertuo capsules or 60 original capsules. Display pods for easy access when it's 7 a.m., you're bleary-eyed, and you've not had your coffee yet.

I've personally reviewed the Subminimal Nanofoamer Go. It's a portable, rechargeable milk frother with detachable heads, also available in an array of cute colors. The best part? It's not just for coffee. I made soufflé eggs and cold foam with this versatile frother.

You'll need to know your loved one's espresso machine portafilter size before purchasing, but that's easily solved by a quick search. Coffee scales may seem super nerdy and over the top, but that's actually not true. Anyone who cares about espresso, even a little bit, will want an espresso scale in their life. Available in seven colors (including the gorgeous pink shade in this article's main image), the AeroPress Clear Color is my go-to manual coffee maker at home. I haven't stopped talking about the Lavazza Tabli since I reviewed it a few weeks ago, and I don't see myself stopping any time soon. This pod coffee machine is unlike anything else I've ever tested. This is a near-perfect machine.

The Fellow EKG Stagg is the kettle for coffee nerds. The gooseneck spout allows for precision pour, ensuring those pour-overs, Americanos, long blacks, and even specialty teas are oh-so perfect.

The Nespresso Vertuo Up is one of Nespresso's cheaper machines, especially considering it has a dedicated "Over Ice" mode for compatible pods. Yes, you can brew hot espresso and cold brew-style drinks with just a push of a button. I gave it an enviable 4 stars in my review.

I've tested over 50 coffee makers — guess how many have received a perfect 5-star rating from me? 3... 2... 1... Okay, did you say one? If you said one, you win! If you said anything else, try again next time. But in all seriousness, this is the only coffee machine I've given a perfect 5 stars. The Breville Bambino is a premium machine wrapped up in a budget package — and it could be the perfect gift for the coffee lover in your life.

The Breville Bambino Plus is another near-perfect espresso machine: this one has automatic milk frothing, ideal if you'd rather kick back and let the machine put in a hard shift, and all the same premium features like a PID controller and customizable pre-infusion as the Bambino.

Does "Mara" translate to "beauty" or something? Because it should. The Lelit Mara X3 is... I mean, just look at it. The floral espresso/steam knobs, the manometer, the brushed metal finish... everything about this machine screams premium. And that's exactly what you'll get. The machine has a customizable steam texture, totally manipulable pressure throughout extraction, and three heat settings. This is a work of art and a talking point.

The Fellow Espresso Series 1 is both a beauty and a hard worker. I awarded it a delicious 4.5 stars in my Fellow Espresso Series 1 review thanks to its delicious espresso, easy UI, and powerful steam wand. If you want to level up from coffee lover to coffee lifestyle-er, this is the machine for you.

#3329. Sean Duffy Says It's Unclear How Router Overloaded ATC System, Doesn't Rule Out Hack

Sean Duffy still doesn't know why one router in Arkansas overloaded the entire air traffic control system, leading to a nationwide ground stop ... but he's not totally ruling out a hack.

The Transportation Secretary addressed the media during a press conference on Tuesday ... and his answer to several key questions didn't inspire much confidence among Americans.

Duffy says they've been able to recreate the overload that occurred in El Dorado, Arkansas, on Friday ... but they can't figure out the root cause of why it happened.

He then goes on to say everyone in intelligence he's spoken to says this isn't a cyberattack or a hack ... but adds that if they find out it was a hack, he'll inform the public promptly.

In simpler terms ... the Department of Transportation knows how to overload the system in El Dorado, but not why it happened, and Duffy's confident this isn't an attack -- but he may change that assessment in the future. Hooray?

We've also spoken to people in the cybersecurity world -- including Harvard lecturer Bruce Schneier, who tells us he doesn't believe this is an attack either ... but instead late-stage capitalism wreaking havoc.

Americans aren't ready to breathe a sigh of relief yet ... with each new issue adding to the country's collective anxiety.

Congress is demanding answers ... but so far it seems like we don't have any.

Don't worry, everyone ... Secretary Duffy is on the case!!!

#3328. Netflix’s ‘Black Doves’ Has the Perfect Solution for James Bond’s Biggest Problem

There are more than a few shows about espionage and spycraft on television right now, and the genre is about to get a major shot of adrenaline on the big screen with the confirmation that Robert Pattinson has been cast as the newest James Bond. Black Doves stands out among other secret agent shows because it portrays more of the characters than just their relationship to government conspiracies and world-ending threats. Being an assassin is a dangerous line of work, but it's also a profession both Helen (Keira Knightley) and Sam (Ben Whishaw) have fallen into and now have no way to escape. Although there are certainly threats that could potentially thrust all of Great Britain — and potentially the entire world — into chaos, the emphasis on grounded characterization is what makes Black Doves such an exhilarating series.

The titular “Black Doves” is an organization of high-ranking assassins who perform covert missions with global implications, and one that Helen is still working for while her husband, Wallace Webb (Andrew Buchan), becomes the Secretary of State for Defense. While Helen struggles to be more open with her loved ones, Sam has the opposite problem; he has never been able to find someone he can have a permanent relationship with, and often chooses isolation to avoid being further devastated. Black Doves shows how spies’ advanced training and perceptiveness come at the cost of other aspects of life, making “normalcy” a foreign concept. It’s among the most action-packed and twisty shows on television right now, but the solid writing provides just as much reason to care for the characters on screen.

Helen is an atypical protagonist for an action show because Black Doves highlights a mother in the middle of a struggling marriage that does not provide an easy solution to her problems. Although she was initially assigned to seduce Wallace and gain information through him for the Black Doves, she develops a genuine attraction to him that ultimately turns into love. The guardedness that Helen shows, leading to her affair with Jason (Andrew Koji) in Season 1, isn't a sign that she is unhappy with Wallace, but that she can't fully open up to someone she can't be honest with. This makes for a fascinating character arc, as Helen is clearly an expert in her field but is made to feel guilty about what she is best at.

Espionage meets the unground world of crime.

Whishaw gives Sam a gritty, worn-down persona that reflects his efforts to bury his emotions and avoid any commitment. Although, in theory, not being tied down to a single person would make Sam less vulnerable to threats, Whishaw is able to show the draining impact this has as his character is forced to give up time with those who might make him happy; Season 2 even introduces a heartbreaking twist when Sam’s duties get in the way of his burgeoning romance with Jerry (Samuel Barnett). This leads to one of the show's most powerful moments, where Sam admits his vulnerabilities to Helen, revealing the strong connection between them, forged by the shared secrets they are forced to keep.

Black Doves goes beyond the clichés of a typical spy story because it provides context and depth to one of its most mysterious characters. Season 1 introduces Elizabeth Reed (Sarah Lancashire) as the most ruthless, brilliant mastermind in the Black Doves organization who serves as a handler for Helen, positioning her in a way similar to Bond's MI6 chief M. Season 2 complicates the character by examining her backstory through an undercover operation in East Berlin that went south. It’s a reminder that there are no clean getaways for those involved in espionage who think they can make a clean break, and the complex dynamic that emerges between Reed and her daughter Vita (Bailey Fines) in the aftermath explores the generational cost of giving up one’s life to duty. Black Doves is able to expose the faults in even its heroic characters; all of them have committed terrible acts in their line of work, and it is up to the audience to determine whether the ends justify the means.

Although its trio of stars makes Black Doves one of the best-acted shows on the air, the ensemble cast is full of great performances that offer more depth to the characters. Season 2 develops an earnest and emotional bond between the assassins Williams (Ella Lily Hyland) and Eleanor (Gabrielle Creevy); while they easily could have been used for little more than comic relief, Black Doves makes a thoughtful point about generations' different priorities by showing how sharply this pair contrasts with Helen and Sam. Just because someone possesses incredible skills doesn’t mean that they aren't also human. Not only is the ability to graft emotional honesty within a series that is so frequently absurd (in the best way) one of Black Doves' biggest achievements, but it's also a storytelling strength that the upcoming James Bond reboot should take a page from.

#3327. iOS 27.2 has two CarPlay improvements, here’s what’s new

iOS 27.2 arrived last month with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.

These changes are related to the broader rebrand of Apple Music that was recently unveiled.

For more new features in CarPlay that debuted in iOS 27, see our coverage here.

Sources with direct knowledge told us Heidi was grieving the loss and surrounded by family and friends during the difficult time.

TP-Link’s Roam routers are compact enough to travel with and let you share a hotel or public internet connection across your devices through a private Wi-Fi network—and right now, Amazon has three models on sale: the Roam 6 AX1500 for $44.99 (was $59.99), the Roam 6 AX3000 for $55.98 (was $79.99), and the Roam 7 BE3600 for $87.99 (was $119.99). #3321. ‘Obsession’ Director’s Next Movie Officially Casts a Stephen King Favorite

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Matthew Lillard, who has now worked on more than a few Stephen King adaptations, has spent enough time in haunted houses to know how badly this can go. In Thir13en Ghosts, he plays one of the few people who understands what’s trapped inside the house, which is a miserable thing to know when everybody else is still getting a tour. A year later, he was Shaggy in Scooby-Doo, trying to survive a trip to a resort where the monsters really did turn out to be monsters. There’s a lot of room between those two performances, and Curry Barker’s next movie sounds like it could use both.

Barker got the biggest horror hit of 2026 out of a guy making one selfish wish. Obsession has cleared $500 million worldwide and arrives on Netflix in the U.S. today, just as its director is adding another familiar face to his next movie. This time, Barker and longtime collaborator Cooper Tomlinson are playing two guys who have made the mistake of telling people they know how to handle a haunting. Eventually, somebody takes them at their word.

Lillard has joined the cast of Curry Barker’s Anything But Ghosts, a horror comedy set in the same universe as Obsession that Focus Features will release in theaters on May 7, 2027. Lillard’s role in the movie currently remains under wraps. He joins Barker, Tomlinson, Aaron Paul, Bryce Dallas Howard, Violet McGraw, and Chris Reinacher.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Barker and Tomlinson play fake ghost hunters who are hired by a couple with an actual ghost problem. Barker directs from a script he wrote with Tomlinson, and putting the two of them in front of the camera gives the movie a different setup from Obsession. They’re the ones who have to stand in somebody’s house and pretend they know what they’re doing, even after they realize their clients have every reason to be scared.

The fun of casting Lillard in Anything But Ghosts is how much of his career already points to how perfect he is for a scenario like the one Barker and Tomlinson have cooked up. He spent two Scooby-Doo movies as the guy who wanted out of the haunted house before anybody had finished explaining why they were there. In Scream, he got one of the movie’s biggest laughs out of Stu realizing he might actually bleed to death. That timing could do a lot for a comedy about two frauds who have to keep up the act once the ghosts show up. Lillard’s more recent work in Mike Flanagan's Carrie and Daredevil: Born Again shows how much darker he can go, and his William Afton in Five Nights at Freddy’s is a reminder that the same guy who’s great at panicking can be just as good at giving everybody else a reason to panic.

Anything But Ghosts premieres in theaters May 7, 2027.

Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3319. Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

Even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

How does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”

Yeah still not my go to navigation option. Maybe in 3-5 years their engineering team will mimic Waze and treat it like they've just discovered something great😒🤣

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple says you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

Test Gemini’s financial know-how with these prompts

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it's time to do a bit of extra research into your finances, AI tools like ChatGPT’s Finances dashboard exist to help you do just that (as long as you trust it enough to connect your financial accounts to it through Plaid).

It doesn’t come as much of a surprise that Gemini has decided to join in on that trend. Google has already begun rolling out Google Wallet as the last connected app to become integrated into Gemini—US users now have the ability to use this feature to get informed responses on their finances based on the linked credit card and bank accounts attached to their Google Wallet profile via Plaid.

Turning Google Wallet on inside Gemini is as simple as clicking on the “Settings” icon (which is the gear wheel that sits across from your Google account name and photo), selecting “Personal Intelligence,” clicking “Connected Apps” and adding the Google Wallet connector. From that point forward, you can prompt the connector by starting your inquiry with “@Google Wallet.”

Thankfully, Gemini’s Google Wallet powers exist only to give you financial insight—it will never move, manage or invest any of the money attached to your linked accounts. To get the best insights, it’s worth trying out any of the following prompts to see just how helpful it can be.

I decided to ask Gemini itself about the sort of basic questions anyone willing to try its Google Wallet-connected app should ask. Google’s chatbot came back to me with a collection of readily usable prompts—here are 10 that you should keep in your digital back pocket for yourself and anyone else you know who might want to try them out for themselves:

The first prompt gets straight to the point, as it scans your linked transaction history to check for any recurring charges and flag any sudden price increases you might have missed.

The second prompt investigates your cash flow, producing a dynamic spending chart while pointing out which purchasing categories you may need to cut back on. The third prompt examines your holiday spending trends from the year prior to see how much you may need to save for the current year’s holiday expenses.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The fourth prompt highlights all the frequent tap-to-pay purchases you might have made on eating out compared to your grocery spending, which could compel you to ease up on dining out so much and look for cheaper alternatives while shopping.

The fifth prompt goes the extra mile to see if any of your linked accounts have any active offers that you can take advantage of before you make a purchase. The sixth prompt makes finding your boarding pass while you’re at a check-in counter and looking up your loyalty numbers while booking a flight so much quicker.

The seventh prompt works across Gemini’s Personal Intelligence “Memory Summary” feature, your connected Google Wallet and your Gmail to compare what you bought (via email receipts) with how much you spent (via bank/card account info). That way, you can see if you're close or far away from meeting the financial goals you’ve told Gemini about.

The eighth prompt works great as a visual aid since Gemini can generate dynamic charts for you and give you an easy-to-follow visualization of how your money is distributed across your checking and savings accounts. The ninth prompt is effective for doing a quick sweep of your accounts to see if there are any anomalies or accidental double charges that have popped up across your linked accounts.

The tenth and final prompt is efficient since it can bring up any stored concert tickets on your Google Wallet while instantly accessing your local transit pass before you use any public transportation to get to your destination.

I’m surprised it took this long for Google to connect its Wallet tool to Gemini, especially since its competitor ChatGPT offers a similar financial tool already.

Nevertheless, it has finally arrived and sticks out as another useful way to utilize AI to give you a clearer picture of your spending habits so you can make more informed decisions about how to save & spend your money. And besides that, it can bring up any other information you need about your linked accounts to make subscription cancellations or whatever other actions you may need to take.

#3315. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3314. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

#3312. HBO's 5-Part Haunting Historical Miniseries Is a True Streaming Masterpiece

There are few miniseries that can actually be considered masterpieces. Some shows are popular at the time they air, but don't hold up once a few years have passed. Of course, there are some limited series that manage to be extraordinary whenever they're viewed. Adolescence, Band of Brothers, Angels in America, and the classic Roots are still every bit as powerful as when they aired. There's one other HBO miniseries that is truly brilliant and can definitely be considered one of the best among these fantastic shows.

Chernobyl is a five-episode limited series that aired in 2019. It is a dramatized version of one of the most significant historical events in recent memory. In 1986, a disaster occurred at the Chernobyl nuclear plant in the town of Pripyat in the Soviet Union, which is now considered Ukraine. In a chilling, heart-racing narrative, the series depicts the events that led up to the meltdown, as well as the harrowing aftermath. Two engineers were killed in the initial explosion, and many others were badly burned. But it became apparent that the dangers Chernobyl exposed were actually much more far-reaching. Many of the plant workers and emergency response team began dying of acute radiation syndrome. Their deaths are portrayed in several excruciating scenes in the series.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The most devastating aspect is that the disaster continued to cause deaths even years later, with one study estimating that a total of nearly 4,000 deaths can now be linked to the meltdown (many from cancer-related illnesses). Chernobyl depicts not only the immediate fallout from the explosion, but also the major cover-up that took place following the event. A brave scientist named Valery Legasov (Jared Harris) tries to share his knowledge of the true breadth of the disaster with the Kremlin, but he is silenced. Because of this denial of the facts, the Soviet Union's choices led to many more deaths. The actual environmental effects from the Chernobyl disaster are still being felt even 40 years later.

Chernobyl, created by Craig Mazin (The Last of Us), is a completely compelling piece of art because it feels easy to get sucked into the haunting storytelling. Every emotion, whether it's bloodcurdling terror or heartbreaking grief, is conveyed effortlessly through the writing, so that you'll feel as though you're a part of the action yourself. Mazin ensures that every decision made by the characters (and their real-life counterparts in turn), whether heroic or calculated, creates a world in which things can never go back to the way they were. The heart-wrenching realism of the narrative makes some of the scenes difficult to watch, especially in their graphic gruesomeness, but this only adds to the authentic nature of the series.

Chernobyl thrives because Mazin is able to showcase so many different perspectives within the framework. One of the most captivating POVs is that of Lyudmilla (Jessie Buckley), the loving wife of one of the brave firefighters who is called to the scene. The range of emotions she experiences during her journey are masterfully displayed, and Buckley ensures that we see the tragic, complex nature of her story. Stellan Skarsgård is fascinating as Boris Scherbina, a chairman of the Kremlin, and Harris is equally transfixing as Valery. Emily Watson portrays Ulana Khomyuk, one of the few characters in the series who is actually fictional. Her fierce devotion to the truth makes her an essential part of the narrative. Harris, Skarsgård, and Watson all received Emmy nominations for their incredible work here, and it's no surprise that viewers were deeply affected by their performances.

History's most exceptional television miniseries.

Chernobyl received plenty of acclaim from critics when it premiered, and managed to take home 10 Emmy wins, including Outstanding Limited Series, and a total of 19 nominations. The series consistently lands on lists of the best miniseries ever made, and upon viewing, it's easy to see why. The realistic depiction of such a world-changing event is handled with historical accuracy and attention to detail, but the humans who were deeply affected by the events that day remain the heart of the storytelling. Whether you're watching Chernobyl for the first time, or are planning a re-watch, you'll have to agree that it has certainly earned its title of masterpiece.

Chernobyl is available to stream on HBO Max in the U.S.

‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Madden’ and more are streaming

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

First up, if you don’t mind forking over a rental/purchase fee, then the biggest arrival is unquestionably the streaming debut of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey.” After a lengthy theatrical run, this $1.8 billion-grossing epic is finally swapping the big screen for at-home streaming. Competing for attention this week is Netflix’s latest seasonal rom-com, Prime Video’s sports biopic based on the life of a football superstar, and a slice-of-life drama on HBO Max that charts a pivot summer for a TV chef. And that's just a taster.

Below I’ve collected together all the new movies on streaming this week, along with some insights into my top picks. Plus, be sure to check out our companion guide covering all the top TV shows you binge-watch this week.

“The Odyssey” finally heads to streaming this week after a four-month run in theaters. In an era where some movies swap the big screen for streaming weeks after release, Christopher Nolan’s acclaimed adaptation of Homer’s timeless poem has bucked the trend. This epic blockbuster deserved to be seen on the biggest screen possible (IMAX preferable), but I’ve no doubt it’ll still be satisfying even when watched on a much smaller television display.

For this fantasy epic, Nolan assembled an all-star cast including Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, Jon Bernthal, Charlize Theron, Elliot Page and more. The flick follows Odysseus (Damon), a hero of the Trojan War, who endures a multi-year odyssey to return home to his native land of Ithaca and reunite with his beloved wife, Penelope (Hathaway), and son, Telemachus (Holland). Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is an epic in every sense of the word, and one of 2026’s very best movies, period.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 18

Netflix’s holiday movie slate is underway, and the next seasonal original under the tree is “Guarding Stars.” This wintry romantic comedy is based on the novel “The Bodyguard” by Katherine Center. It focuses on a fake relationship that, to the surprise of literally nobody, quickly blossoms into the real thing. This one definitely doesn't have future Christmas classic written all over it based on the trailer, but it might be good for two hours of festive fun.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Jack Stapleton (Jared Padalecki) is an A-lister action star heading home for the holidays while also trying to dodge the unwanted advances of a very committed stalker. In steps no-nonsense bodyguard Hannah Brooks (Leighton Meester), and because this is a rom-com, the two pretend to be a couple so the actor’s family doesn’t worry about his safety. What starts as a fake relationship heats up over the holidays and becomes a real romance.

Thanksgiving is synonymous with watching football, so in the run-up to Turkey Day, Prime Video is debuting its new biographical sports movie, “Madden.” You probably don’t need any clues to know which football icon this David O. Russell film revolves around. That would be John Madden (duh!), the Super Bowl-winning coach, beloved commentator, and the man who lent his name to the best-selling EA Sports video game series Madden.

Nicolas Cage plays Madden, with Christian Bale (a frequent collaborator with O. Russell) playing his best friend and Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis. Kathryn Hahn features as John’s wife, Virginia Fields. This biopic chronicles Madden’s incredible career in the game, as he became the sport's most recognizable voice, and worked with EA Sports to build a video game dynasty. It’s a celebration of spirit, friendship, and a love of the game that made Madden an enduring American icon.

Watch on Prime Video starting November 18

Speaking of biopics that offer insight into an American icon, “Tony” is heading to HBO Max this week. This coming-of-age comedy-drama chronicles a defining summer in the life of celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain (played here by Dominic Sessa). Rather than trying to cover Bourdain’s entire life or career, “Tony” is a slice-of-life picture set over a single transformative summer. This narrative decision adds intimacy and a delightful richness.

Set in 1975, Anthony Bourdain, going by Tony, is an arrogant student at Vassar College. By his own admission, he's "badly in need of a good ass-kicking." Dreaming of becoming a writer, he follows his high school crush (Emilia Jones) to Provincetown, Massachusetts. In need of a place to stay, he finds himself working in a Cape Cod kitchen under the watch of head chef José Vatel (Antonio Banderas), and develops a passion for the culinary arts that would shape the course of his life. Sessa is excellent, as is Banderas, and best of all, “Tony” is an incredibly warm movie, perfect for cold winter nights.

Disney is gearing up for the release of its tentpole animated movie for the Thanksgiving season, “Hexed.” But if the eye-watering cost of taking a whole family to the theater is already making your wallet shed tears, “Steps” on Netflix might be a suitable lower-cost alternative. This animated fantasy musical looks like a whimsical adventure for all ages, and because it puts a new twist on a well-known fairy tale, it definitely has a Disney-ish quality.

Like many modern animated movies, “Steps” puts a new spin on a timeless tale, in this case, Cinderella. Here, Cinders (voiced by Amanda Seyfried) teams up with Lilith (Ali Wong), one of her misunderstood stepsisters. When Lilith steals the Fairy Godmother’s wand, she accidentally transforms the other stepsister into a frog, and in the chaos, the mean-spirited Priscilla (Nikki Glaser) takes the kingdom’s throne. Now, the unlikely, squabbling pair must team up to save the day and prove that even a "villain" can be a hero.

#3308. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3307. iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day

iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

"iOS 27.3 adds three new features I've used almost every day", "Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving". What's with these terrible clickbait titles lately? Did we go back to 2014?

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

Read more: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love
